snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.subtitle: The dogmatist error Nietzsche opens against
snapshots.body: Named in the opening of the Preface as the author of the most dangerous of all errors — the invention of Pure Spirit and the Good in Itself — which Nietzsche treats as the founding mistake of European philosophy, a kind of noble sickness inherited from Socrates.

snapshots.name: Immanuel Kant
snapshots.subtitle: Critiqued for hidden vanity
snapshots.body: The philosopher Nietzsche accuses, in Chapter I, of a kind of theological sleight of hand — smuggling old metaphysical commitments back in through his Table of Categories and his question of how synthetic judgments a priori are possible, while priding himself on having escaped dogmatism.

snapshots.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
snapshots.subtitle: Nietzsche's early master, now doubted
snapshots.body: The philosopher of the Will whose claim that "I will" is an immediate certainty, and that the will alone is truly known, Nietzsche subjects to close scrutiny in Chapter I, arguing that willing is in fact a far more complicated and unexamined process than Schopenhauer's superstition allowed.

snapshots.name: Blaise Pascal
snapshots.subtitle: The Christian conscience Nietzsche measures himself against
snapshots.body: Invoked in "The Religious Mood" as the model of a terrible, self-annihilating Christian faith — a continuous, slow suicide of reason for the sake of a fundamental and irreducible perversion of the will, which Nietzsche treats with more respect than contempt.

snapshots.name: Richard Wagner
snapshots.subtitle: The composer haunting the later chapters
snapshots.body: The composer Nietzsche once revered, mentioned repeatedly in the book's second half — from the Meistersinger overture in "Peoples and Countries" to a passing, unflattering sketch of a devoted Wagnerienne — as an example of German art's late, heavy grandeur.

snapshots.name: The Will to Power
snapshots.subtitle: Nietzsche's fundamental drive
snapshots.body: The force Nietzsche proposes underlies philosophy itself and, more broadly, all organic life: not mere self-preservation but a tyrannical, world-creating impulse to appropriate, dominate, and grow — first named in Chapter II and advanced as a thesis in Chapter III.

snapshots.name: Master-Morality and Slave-Morality
snapshots.subtitle: Two moral types, section 260
snapshots.body: The distinction Nietzsche draws in Chapter IX between values that originate in a ruling caste proud of its difference from the ruled, and values that originate among the ruled and dependent — two moralities that mix, misunderstand, and sometimes clash within a single soul.

snapshots.name: The Free Spirit
snapshots.subtitle: Nietzsche's philosopher of the future
snapshots.body: The figure Chapter II is devoted to: a thinker unbound from the prejudices of dogmatism and herd conviction, who Nietzsche insists will not be merely free but something more — his imagined vanguard for the philosophy still to come.

snapshots.name: The Herd (Herd Instinct)
snapshots.subtitle: What Nietzsche calls conscience
snapshots.body: Nietzsche's name, in Chapter V, for the moral instinct of obedience that has triumphed throughout human history in family alliances, tribes, and states — what Christians call faith, and what Nietzsche bluntly renames "the herd."

snapshots.name: The Order of Rank
snapshots.subtitle: What is noble?
snapshots.body: The organizing idea of Chapter IX: that souls and types of men stand in an unalterable, innate hierarchy of value, and that the noble type distinguishes itself precisely by this instinct for rank and distance from what it takes to be lower.
